title: Named case study, minimalist verdict
principle: Give away the secrets, sell the implementation. People don't buy information, they buy an experienced head that gets it right the first time.
best_for: service providers proving craft judgement. Name the client where you have permission; anonymised case studies invite the "this sounds made up" objection.
requires: a named client and their specific starting requirements plus the outcome achieved
hook: Some [group/clients] don't need [expected element]. / [Person's name] is one of them.

title: Before/after, "here's what I actually changed"
principle: Every product or service must deliver a transformation. Sell the transformation, not the thing.
best_for: a founder who improved their own metric and can show the specific moves.
requires: their own specific starting/improved metrics and the exact changes they made
hook: I went from [starting metric] to [improved metric]. / Here's what I actually changed:

title: The Escalating Proof Ladder
principle: Stack evidence in order of increasing scale and authority. Save the strongest proof for last, like a crescendo. Also works for stacking pain points or story beats to build tension.
best_for: a bold market prediction the prospect actually holds.
requires: five specific real numbers, actions, or events proving the trend/prediction
hook: I couldn't possibly be any more bullish on [industry/trend] right now: / > [Example 1: include specific numbers/actions/key events]

title: Deliberate alienation
principle: Call out explicitly who the content is for and who it isn't. Make people pick a side. Writing for everyone is writing for no one. Content should repel as well as attract.
best_for: a founder with a clear offer and a dismissive-outsider story to tell.
requires: the exact dismissive question an old acquaintance asked and the turning point since
hook: I caught up with an old [acquaintance] recently and they asked me "[Dismissive question]?" / These days I don't get offended or try to prove anything when people from my past life think [pursuit] is just some side hobby.

title: Comment-gated lead magnet
principle: The tactic still works; what people hate is the worthless resource behind it. Hormozi's lead magnet rules apply: pick one narrow problem and solve it completely, make it good enough to have charged for, deliver a win they feel in minutes.
best_for: prospects with a genuine asset to give away. Skip if the resource is thin.
requires: specific dollar amounts spent, resulting income/metrics, and a real resource to give away
hook: The [tool/asset] behind my [project] cost me [small dollar amount]. [Brief anecdote about what you did to acquire it/start]. / [Self-deprecating detail about not knowing something a novice wouldn't know].

title: Build-in-public / document don't create
principle: Three questions are an endless idea source: what am I building, what did I ship last week, what problem am I solving for myself. Sharing the mission gives people a reason to keep following.
best_for: founders shipping something visible.
requires: the specific tools used, product shipped, and an earlier simpler version built
hook: I made this [type of output] using only [tool 1] & [tool 2]. / (this isn't a "[category] is dead" [asset]).

title: "The jobs that made us"
principle: First jobs are a universal experience. Tap shared relatability to widen reach.
best_for: any prospect with a non-obvious career origin. Strong opener for a founder who came from a trade or an unrelated field, which makes it a good fit for obscure niches.
requires: a specific first job and a memorable detail or lesson from it
hook: The jobs that made us… [time period] ago, I was a [past role/job]. Things I learned that stick with me today: / This pic is from [reference to the image or artifact tied to the story]. I had [lack of skill/experience], no professional clue what I was doing, and a [dream/goal].

title: One habit, one outcome
principle: "Incubation" — the subconscious keeps working while you're not actively thinking. Also: switching between two or three projects every couple of hours lets one nourish another.
best_for: an operator with a specific repeatable ritual.
requires: a specific achieved outcome/metric and the exact single habit that produced it
hook: I [achieved impressive outcome]. / From ONE simple habit:

title: A vs B comparison
principle: Comparison posts invite disagreement, which drives comments, and imply a verdict, which aids decisions. Lead with the verdict in the hook rather than withholding it — that provokes the "why?" and creates curiosity.
best_for: a prospect with a real tool, vendor, or method switch to report. Very strong in technical or trade niches where buyers compare constantly.
requires: two specific tools/methods compared with real prices, observations, and a stated verdict
hook: I [made surprising product choice - e.g. downgrade]. / Here's what happened:

title: Micro-moment, macro-lesson
principle: A 14-word exchange can carry a full lesson. Notice small moments, reflect, and put yourself into the content.
best_for: the highest-ceiling template here and the hardest to fake. Only use where research surfaced a real anecdote. Do not invent the moment.
requires: a real quoted exchange/moment that cannot be invented, plus their actual reply
hook: I [describe scene where someone says or does something that triggers a reaction in you]: / "[Quote the exact phrase that triggered it]"

title: What a post written by an actual human looks like…
principle: Quirky, hyper-specific personal facts (not polished positioning language) are what make a post read as unmistakably human — that specificity is exactly what generic AI-sounding content lacks.
best_for: founders/personal brand builders who want a definitive "about me" post that differentiates them from bland, AI-flavored LinkedIn content, backed by real client results.
requires: real age, birthplace, quirky personal facts, and named client results
hook: I'm [age]. Born in [place]. Raised in [place]. Now live in [place]. I [profession/role in one line] and I run a business with [person OR include another interesting fact about your business]. / - [quirky personal fact 1]

title: Apply this "everyone wants X, nobody wants Y" thesis hook to almost any domain
principle: People want the big outcome but resist paying the real price for it; naming a specific authority/data source instead of vague stats lends the contrarian thesis instant credibility.
best_for: analysts and educators who can cite named studies or data to challenge a comfortable assumption their audience holds about success.
requires: a named study/authority and its specific data findings that contradict an assumption
hook: Everyone wants [desirable outcome]. / Nobody wants to do what it actually takes.

title: The Contrarian Spotlight
principle: Challenging a popular opinion in your niche gives readers a fresh perspective to grapple with and sparks debate in the comments — disagreement is a sign you said something conversation-worthy, not a problem to avoid.
best_for: scrappy operators who can back a contrarian claim with concrete, low-cost alternatives and real numbers rather than just being edgy for its own sake.
requires: specific low-cost alternatives used with actual costs and outcomes achieved
hook: [Contrarian claim about what's not required to succeed]. / I think we use that as a crutch - oh yeah sure, I'd do that too if I had [common excuse/resource].

title: The Value-First Method (event promotion)
principle: Lead an event promo with a genuinely useful framework instead of a bare "come to my event" pitch, so the post pays off for the reader whether or not they register.
best_for: coaches and consultants promoting a webinar, cohort, or event who want the promo post to also double as proof of their expertise.
requires: a real experience/volume credibility marker and one quantified negative consequence example
hook: After [credibility marker: scale/volume of experience], I can tell you the difference between the ones that [negative outcome] and the ones that [positive outcome] comes down to these [X] levers. / Every [type of entity] needs:

title: The proof-stacked authority pitch
principle: Every high-performing post in this issue leans on proof — named client results, cited data, or a documented track record — because new readers are always silently asking "why should I listen to you?"
best_for: experts selling a premium or specialized service who need to justify a high price point to an audience meeting them for the first time.
requires: specific service price, years to scale, and real income figures achieved
hook: People are paying [profession] $[dollar amount]/[time period] for this one, in-demand [service/skill]: / [Service name].

title: Turn life's calamities into business lessons
principle: This taps "The Pratfall Effect" — people perceive you as more likeable when you reveal a blunder, flaw, or misfortune, so an honest bad-news post stands out in a feed full of wins and "proud" announcements.
best_for: service providers or founders comfortable admitting a messy, chaotic moment in real time — good for prospects whose brand feels too polished and needs a relatable, human crack in the armor.
requires: a specific real chaotic situation happening in their business right now
hook: [Common cliché phrase/joke from your industry]: / [your honest reaction to that phrase]

title: How to HAMMER an idea into people's heads
principle: Repeating a core motif in multiple different phrasings is persuasive — it shows conviction and increases the odds your central message actually lands and gets remembered.
best_for: founders or experts trying to build one "ownable idea" — best suited to prospects who already have a strong, bold operating belief they want to become known for.
requires: the specific thing built in public and specific actions/topics deliberately skipped
hook: Most people are [common, watered-down behavior in your field]. / They [example 1].

title: The case for getting personal on LinkedIn
principle: Not every post needs to be ROI-positive — a personal post that shows you're an actual human being helps you cut through, reach more people, and build affiliation, which ultimately benefits the business anyway.
best_for: clients who post only stiff, business-only content — good for loosening up a founder's voice and giving prospects an easy ice-breaker into a real conversation.
requires: five real personal facts/hobbies not previously shared on their LinkedIn
hook: [X] things you probably wouldn't know about me from my LinkedIn: / 1. [Personal interest/hobby/fact/realization 1]

title: Why you should give more examples
principle: Examples do the heavy lifting in educational content — they make abstract advice concrete, act as receipts behind a claim, and let you teach the same idea in fresh ways.
best_for: experts with a repeatable evaluative process (portfolio reviews, audits, critiques) who can open up a real, transparent activity instead of giving abstract advice.
requires: a specific transparent public activity/event they ran and real observations from it
hook: I've [done a specific, high-volume action] in [timeframe]. / But on [day/date], [X] people watched me [do an unusual, transparent activity] for [duration] so they know exactly what I [look for/do/think] when I [related everyday action].

title: The news hook (steal urgency & borrow authority)
principle: Time-stamped events, jarring numbers, and well-known company names emotionally charge an argument with fear and urgency — borrowing authority from a notable name boosts reach beyond a generic advice post.
best_for: career or business-advice prospects who want to ride a breaking-news moment into a timely, high-reach post that ends in a clear recommendation.
requires: real recent news events/company names and the specific consequences to cite
hook: [Fact 1: a negative event, stated plainly]. / [Fact 2: a contrasting event soon after].

title: The "recently someone asked me" post
principle: Banking recurring audience questions gives you pre-validated content — if one person asks, others are silently wondering the same thing, and a strong answer becomes reusable material forever.
best_for: consultants and coaches who take a lot of discovery or client calls and can mine call transcripts for the same question resurfacing again and again.
requires: a real recurring question a client actually asked them
hook: I've [brief proof point establishing years of experience]. Now I [desirable lifestyle outcome]. / But recently someone asked me "[relatable question about achieving that outcome]?"

title: It's your job as a creator to do THIS…
principle: Correcting a faulty belief gives the reader a small dopamine hit ("that's not how I was told the world worked") and positions the writer as an insider on the reader's side against an outdated assumption.
best_for: experts with first-hand visibility into a shifting industry practice (hiring, buying, evaluation criteria) who can credibly name what's replaced the old priority.
requires: general industry insight into what evaluators actually prioritize now, no personal facts
hook: [Role/group] won't tell you this. / But it's real. [Common belief] does not matter... as much as it used to [timeframe].

title: A cheeky way to maximize reach once (or twice) a year
principle: Birthdays and anniversaries are near-universal reach triggers — people can't resist acknowledging a milestone, so naming the occasion in your hook borrows that built-in engagement, and mixing lowlights with highlights keeps it relatable rather than boastful.
best_for: clients with a personal or company milestone coming up (birthday, work anniversary, founding date) who want a low-effort, high-reach reflective post.
requires: real personal achievements and honest missed goals from a specific year
hook: I'm [age or milestone marker]. Here's some highlights from being [previous age or stage]: / - [Achievement/milestone/remarkable event 1]

title: The secret to creating content that resonates
principle: Ideas validated live — a keynote reaction, a client's surprised response — are pre-tested; if a point lands in person, it will likely land online too, so mine real-time reactions instead of guessing what to post.
best_for: speakers, consultants, or founders who present or pitch regularly and can point to a specific moment where a live audience visibly reacted to an idea.
requires: a specific real presentation moment and the audience's actual live reaction
hook: I [briefly describe showing or presenting something - set the scene, don't reveal] and [describe surprising/positive feedback]. / It was a simple comparison:

title: Struggling to book calls?
principle: Personalized, effort-heavy outreach (like custom video DMs) beats generic templates because it visibly proves the sender did the research — pairing a repeatable outreach system with your content compounds pipeline over time.
best_for: prospects who do or want to do direct outreach alongside their content — strong for service providers who want a post that doubles as proof of their exact booked-calls system.
requires: a specific historical result/metric and the exact outreach system steps used
hook: Back in [year], [my business / I] [achieved a specific, concrete result] consistently. We never [common assumption about how that result happens], but [the actual system] worked like crazy: / Every [time period], we'd [first step you took]. Then we'd [second step that involves examples]:

title: Your content needs an enemy
principle: Conflict sparks curiosity — a story (and a brand) is only as good as its villain, so pitting your idea against a clear enemy makes your position instantly legible and shareable.
best_for: founders or experts with a clear contrarian stance against an industry norm or "old way" of doing things — good for sharpening a fuzzy positioning into a memorable us-vs-them frame.
requires: only a contrarian positioning stance and decision criteria, no personal facts
hook: I've [verb] [negative quality] [subject/role] from [specific context]. / I've [verb] [positive quality] [subject/role] from [specific context].

title: The key to emotional storytelling
principle: Sharing your raw internal dialogue — not just the outcome — makes the reader feel the moment instead of just hearing about it; contrasting the reactive first thought with the corrected second thought builds real emotional resonance.
best_for: clients willing to admit a moment of self-doubt or defensiveness before making a good decision — strong for founders or leaders proving they made a hard, purposeful call.
requires: a specific decision/moment and the writer's raw first-thought vs corrected-thought reaction
hook: I [made a decision that signals self-awareness]. / First thing [that happened challenged your existing approach].

title: Different is better than Better
principle: Claiming you're "better" invites direct comparison and commoditizes you; claiming you're different is what actually makes you stand out, because it can't be benchmarked against anyone else.
best_for: prospects competing in a crowded, me-too market who need a differentiated brand stance instead of a features-and-benefits pitch.
requires: a specific recent achievement and the concrete result number it reached
hook: Sorry to tell you this BUT... / You're [provocative quality].

title: One of the most powerful (but underused) tactics in personal branding
principle: Naming and repeating a unique concept for a common problem builds trust and authority — it proves you're an astute observer of your field, and a dramatic, named-concept case study sells your judgment better than any feature list.
best_for: coaches or consultants with a signature framework or named methodology and a client transformation story they have explicit permission to share.
requires: a specific named-concept client transformation story with real quotes and dialogue
hook: My client [dramatic before situation]. [Timeframe] later, [dramatic after situation]. / [They were a person from a specific background] who [context that sets up the challenge].

title: Your POV doesn't just attract customers
principle: Stating plainly what you don't optimize for — and what you do — signals values-driven decision-making, which attracts both the right customers and the right talent into your orbit.
best_for: founders or leaders hiring publicly or building a team-facing brand — useful for prospects who want their content to double as a recruiting and culture signal, not just a sales one.
requires: only a stated values/hiring philosophy, no personal facts or client specifics
hook: I don't care [about the conventional metric everyone defaults to]. / [Scenario 1]? [Short neutral acceptance].

title: Tweet-style hook opener
principle: Tweet-format hooks act as attention-grabbing billboards that take up more feed real estate and read in seconds — the format works even if you don't use X, and it doubles as a subtle plug for your own offer.
best_for: creators or service providers who want a fast, low-effort opening hook and a natural way to plug their own site or service without a hard sell.
requires: only a domain method/tactic explanation, no personal or client specifics
hook: My favorite way to do this: / (By far)

title: Failure-first vulnerability post
principle: Audiences don't build true fandom (people who buy) around curated perfection — they relate to how you navigated your worst moments, so failure is an asset, not something to hide.
best_for: founders or coaches building a personal brand who need to differentiate from polished "acting perfect" competitors and convert followers into buyers.
requires: a specific personal failure streak, the pivot made, and the measurable result after
hook: I [vulnerable admission that highlights common pain point]. / [X years of relevant credentials/actions]. [Y credential/actions]. But [0 result].

title: Non-sponsored tool/method recommendation
principle: A value-first, "not sponsored" recommendation with a reusable prompt or method and named results reads as credible precisely because it has no obvious sales angle.
best_for: consultants and marketers building authority around research or process skills who want to demonstrate expertise without pitching a service directly.
requires: a specific tool/resource name, the exact reusable prompt, and specific results gotten
hook: I really think "[tool/resource]" is the most underrated [category] right now. And it's completely [free/accessible]. / Here's my favorite [prompt/method] for [desired outcome]:

title: Curated book-lesson listicle
principle: In the AI era, curating and distilling what you learn still builds authority because most people won't do the reading (or the synthesis) themselves.
best_for: thought-leader-style prospects (coaches, consultants) who consume a lot of books/podcasts and want a low-lift, credibility-building post that doesn't require original client results.
requires: book titles/authors and quotes, no personal facts about the writer needed
hook: I've read [X]+ books on [topic]. Here are [X] of the most important lessons I have learned and applied to my [life/business/scenario]: / 1. "[Quote/Lesson 1]."

title: Lead magnet giveaway (viral comment-to-DM)
principle: Perceived value of a lead magnet comes from stacking social proof, curiosity-driving teaser bullets, and an exclusivity reframe on top of the offer itself — not the offer alone.
best_for: service providers and course creators launching a lead magnet who need a high-volume comment-to-DM mechanism from a single post.
requires: several specific dollar results/outcomes and the percentage tied to one method
note: structurally similar to T18.5 (comment-gated lead magnet) — same "stack proof, tease value, gate behind a comment keyword" mechanic. Use this version when the hook needs to open on a portfolio of results rather than a single asset's cost.
hook: We've had [X] different [result-level] [outcomes] in [year]: / - [Item 1]: [$ amount/result]

title: The "boring truth" framework reveal
principle: Naming your advice "boring" breaks the pattern of hype-driven claims ("hacks," "secrets") and signals rare honesty, which lowers the reader's scepticism and guard.
best_for: consultants or operators with a repeatable system who want to stand out from hype-driven competitors by leaning into unsexy-but-effective positioning.
requires: a named recurring framework and the specific impressive result it generates
hook: The following advice is boring. / But it [generates impressive result for me] every [time period].

title: Generic-lessons authority listicle
principle: The lessons don't need to be original — authority is built through the specific actions, mistakes, and stories behind how you arrived at each one.
best_for: founders or operators sharing a recent milestone (raise, launch, exit) who want a listicle that builds credibility through lived detail rather than generic advice.
requires: a specific achievement built plus personal anecdotes/mistakes behind each numbered lesson
note: echoes T13.4's "client case study" numbered-lesson mechanic but applied to the writer's own milestone rather than a client's transformation.
hook: How I built a [specific achievement] in [timeframe]. / (And [X] lessons I learnt along the way)

title: Social-proof-led event promotion
principle: Readers silently ask "why should I listen to you?" — leading with social proof (in both post copy and image) answers that objection before the pitch for an event or offer lands.
best_for: prospects launching a webinar, workshop, or paid live event who need to establish credibility fast before asking for a registration.
requires: a specific starting goal, the dramatically larger result, and the percentage tied to it
note: echoes T16.4's "value-first event promotion" mechanic — this version leads harder on social proof/numbers before the framework, T16.4 leads with the framework itself.
hook: I started [activity] to get to [modest original goal]. / Fast forward [timeframe], it got me to [dramatically larger result].

title: Polarizing belief / permission-to-be-bold post
principle: Bland, people-pleasing content gets ignored in a crowded feed — being polarizing (without being hateful) about a real belief is what earns attention and conviction-based followers.
best_for: founders or experts with a strong, defensible opinion who are currently playing it safe and need a structure for a bolder, belief-driven post.
requires: a specific years-long false belief the writer held and the moment it was disproven
hook: [Bold universal claim about what's possible or what's true]. / That's the uncomfortable truth most people never figure out.

title: Free-strategy case study to sell a service
principle: Giving away your strategy for free builds trust because people pay for implementation, not information — a named client case study with a clear before/process/after sells harder than a direct pitch.
best_for: service providers (consultants, agencies, coaches) with at least one strong client result who want a soft-sell format that closes with a natural CTA rather than a hard pitch.
requires: a client's specific starting problem, the process used, and the specific result achieved
note: echoes T18.1's "give away the secrets, sell the implementation" principle — this version is process-driven (numbered steps) rather than minimalist-verdict driven.
hook: When I [do service] for [client type], here's how I make sure [I achieve desirable outcome]. / A [client type - e.g. "founder"] reached out to me [time period ago] because they'd been [doing the thing] for [timeframe], had [positive quality], but [state problem] - and couldn't figure out why.

title: Future pacing transformation post
principle: Future pacing projects the reader's life forward and paints a vivid, emotional picture of what's possible (or what to avoid) — feelings drive action more than facts alone.
best_for: coaches and consultants selling transformation-based offers who want the payoff of their advice to feel emotionally real and urgent.
requires: only an imagined future-state narrative, no personal facts or client specifics
hook: This will blow your mind... / It's [time frame] from now and you're:

title: Reactive "scroll with intention" opinion post
principle: Scrolling with intention turns wasted time into raw material — spotting a viral exchange elsewhere and reacting with your own unique take is a fast, low-effort way to generate original content.
best_for: prospects who struggle with idea generation and already spend time browsing social platforms; especially useful for reactive, opinion-based posting.
requires: a specific real piece of content or interaction the writer recently observed
hook: I might get crucified for this, but oh well. / I saw [a piece of content / interaction / moment] recently and it got me thinking.

title: Transformation story as case study
principle: A "back then vs now" transformation story attracts like-minded people by showing the human behind the content, and doubles as a case study when it ties directly to your service offer.
best_for: service providers and founders with a personal transformation story (career pivot, business turnaround) that overlaps with the outcome they now sell to clients.
requires: a specific dated life/business decision and the concrete milestones since
note: echoes T18.2's before/after transformation mechanic — this version is milestone-driven (a specific past date) rather than metric-driven.
hook: In [specific month and year], I [made a significant life or business decision] with [humanising personal detail]. / It's [current year]. Here's where we are now:

title: Bare testimonial screenshot
principle: A single, unembellished testimonial screenshot paired with a short, confident caption is more persuasive than any amount of self-promotion — let the happy customer do the selling.
best_for: service providers who have at least one strong client testimonial and want a near-zero-effort, high-conversion post for slow content weeks.
requires: an actual client testimonial screenshot to paste in as the post
hook: I love my job. / [Screenshot of positive testimonial/feedback from client].

title: Permission-giving contrarian post
principle: Readers often already know what to do — what's holding them back is a limiting belief. Naming and dismantling that belief (rather than teaching another how-to) removes the real barrier to action.
best_for: coaches or consultants whose offer requires a mindset shift (around money, worthiness, time) before the client will act.
requires: only a contrarian mindset stance, no personal facts or client specifics
hook: Oddly unpopular take: / [Core contrarian stance].

title: All scroll-stopping images do THIS
principle: A pattern-interrupt visual paired with a reflective identity narrative earns attention, and a practical payoff (self-assessment questions) makes it worth sharing.
best_for: coaches and consultants building a personal narrative around an unconventional life or career choice — anyone whose authority rests on being "walking proof" of a decision others still question.
requires: a specific judged personal identity/choice and how it changed the writer's life
hook: Just because you [fit/qualify/check the boxes], doesn't mean you [belong/should stay/are in the right place]. / I'm a proud [identity that others might judge].

title: The Midwit Razor is (still) undefeated
principle: Mapping a specific industry observation onto an already-familiar viral meme format maximizes reach, then the "idiot and genius agree" punchline delivers a contrarian insight that a rebrand is just the same old tactic.
best_for: consultants and strategists who want to cut through a buzzword-driven rebrand trend in their industry and position themselves as veterans who've seen the "new" idea before.
requires: only an industry-trend critique and the writer's own take, no personal facts
hook: [Familiar concept] has been getting a rebrand for months. / [New name 1], [New name 2], [New name 3], ...

title: The "Proof, Confession, Pitch" post framework
principle: Ads read as ads and get ignored; leading with proof and a relatable confession earns the reader's trust before the pitch ever shows up, so the endorsement blends into the feed organically.
best_for: prospects promoting their own offer or an affiliate/sponsor deal who need a soft-sell structure that doesn't scream "this is an ad."
requires: a specific achievement number, specific embarrassing audit findings, and a product link
hook: I [impressive achievement] in [short timeframe]. / [Second proof point that escalates the first].

title: Only ONE person reads your content
principle: Every impression is just one pair of eyes, so writing directly to that one reader ("you," "your") makes content feel personal and outperforms writing for an imagined crowd.
best_for: founders and experts who want an evergreen, values-driven post reminding their audience that human connection beats chasing algorithm mechanics.
requires: only a values-driven reframe about human connection, no personal facts
hook: Stop [doing the common thing]. Start [doing alternative thing]. / We've become obsessed with [behaviour].

title: The No.1 rule when making predictions
principle: A prediction only earns trust when it's backed by evidence — and a narrative arc showing you dismissed the trend early, then came around and profited, is more persuasive evidence than any stat.
best_for: founders or experts positioning themselves as early-market voices — ideal for someone with an "I was wrong, then I was early" story to lend weight to their current authority.
requires: a specific dollar figure once offered and the writer's year-by-year skepticism-to-belief story
note: echoes T15.5's "borrow authority via time-stamped/news events" mechanic, but T9.5 uses the writer's own past skepticism as the proof instead of an external news hook.
hook: I remember being shocked that [people/brands] used to offer me [dollar figure] for [thing]. Now I charge a LOT more than that. Here's the full story: / [Year] was when I first saw [peers/others] [doing the new thing]. I told myself [dismissive rationalisation]. This would pass. That I didn't need to chase it.

title: Why this viral post is so damn satisfying
principle: A fear-and-outrage hook ("X is dead") draws the crowd in, then a wall of counter-evidence flips them into vindicated insiders who feel smug enough to repost and forward it to colleagues.
best_for: prospects in an industry that's constantly declared "dead" (SaaS, agencies, cold email) who want to rally their community and position themselves as veterans who've outlasted false predictions before.
requires: researched examples of past failed "industry is dying" predictions, including one dated named-figure quote
hook: [Industry/concept] has been dying since [year]. / Some notable "deaths" include:

title: An underrated reason to build a LinkedIn audience in 2026
principle: Asking your audience to vote on a real decision (instead of only sharing opinions) shows genuine respect for their input and drives far more comments than a standard announcement post.
best_for: founders or product people launching something new (merch, a feature, an event) who want a low-effort, high-engagement post that doubles as crowdsourced market research.
requires: a real upcoming product/decision launch and the specific options being voted on
hook: We're about to [commit to a major production/business decision]. / Help us not screw it up.

title: How to breathe life into dead hooks
principle: An abstract problem statement is lifeless; anchoring the hook in the exact moment the problem became painfully real makes the reader recognize themselves instantly, because it's specific instead of generic.
best_for: SaaS founders or consultants pitching a before/after solution story — especially finance, ops, or workflow tools with a specific "gotcha" moment prospects have all lived through.
requires: past attempts/tools tried, the specific tool/method used, and comparative results vs an incumbent
hook: If you've ever [experienced a specific painful consequence of a known problem], you know the feeling. / [Thing that was supposed to prevent it] said everything was fine.

title: The best ads don't look like ads
principle: The most effective product endorsements read as a personal lesson learned, not a pitch — burying the plug ten sentences deep behind a relatable failure story earns trust before the sell.
best_for: consultants or product owners running a sponsored or affiliate post who need an organic-feeling structure that doesn't announce itself as an ad.
requires: the specific failed actions they took and the product feature that fixed the root cause
note: echoes T9.3's "Proof, Confession, Pitch" mechanic — this version opens directly on an unpopular opinion rather than a proof point.
hook: my unpopular opinion for today:  / most [common activity] fails before [the part everyone focuses on] is even [seen/read/heard].

title: Quick tip to hold your reader's attention
principle: Short suspense phrases ("That's where the opportunity is," "So what does this mean for you?") open and close curiosity loops throughout a post, keeping readers scrolling instead of bouncing.
best_for: writers and consultants making a systemic argument (e.g., "you're optimizing the wrong thing") who need to sustain attention across a longer post.
requires: only a general industry principle/metaphor about over-optimization, no personal or client specifics
hook: You [over-optimised] [thing] so much it [negative metaphor]. / Now it [negative consequence 1].

title: The Daddy of all lead magnets
principle: Packaging your greatest-hits frameworks — rather than creating something new — turns low-effort curation into a comprehensive, rare, and hard-to-replicate lead magnet.
best_for: consultants and coaches who've already shared dozens of frameworks piecemeal and want to consolidate authority into one flagship downloadable asset for lead capture.
requires: their own list of previously shared frameworks and a working download link
note: echoes T18.5's comment-gated lead magnet mechanic, but this version is framed as a "one-pager of everything" rather than a low-cost tool/asset story.
hook: A full [topic] in one page. / Here's what's inside:

title: Get outsized reach with this simple post type
principle: Documenting your real, in-progress use of AI (what's worked, what hasn't, what you wish you could do) cuts through generic "how-to-AI" content and predictions because it's specific and honest rather than expert posturing.
best_for: founders and operators using AI inside their business who want relatable, high-reach content without needing to pose as an AI guru.
requires: three specific real AI systems/processes they've built and the business metric achieved
note: echoes T7.1 (this issue's own framework) loosely and T18.3's "Escalating Proof Ladder" quote-stacking mechanic, applied to AI systems instead of market bullishness.
hook: How I'm using AI to run a [impressive metric] [business type] with [team size - _optional_]: / > [First system/process/initiative you've built - briefly explain how it works and how it's impacting your business].

title: Using AI to create content is not the real problem
principle: Taking a contrarian "I don't care if X" stance and anchoring it in who you actually serve reframes a controversial opinion as principled positioning rather than provocation.
best_for: service providers or tool builders facing backlash over a "controversial" method (e.g., using AI) who need to defend their approach by centering client outcomes over purity debates.
requires: a specific stated controversial opinion and how it applies to each client type served
hook: Unpopular opinion: / I don't care if [controversial thing].

title: An underrated hook that turns your post into a puzzle
principle: A visual guessing game turns passive scrollers into active participants who must click "...see more" to resolve the curiosity loop, then rewards them with a memorable, ownable named concept.
best_for: consultants and strategists who've coined (or want to coin) a proprietary framework and need a high-engagement way to introduce it.
requires: a named proprietary framework, its illustrative examples, and a specific client result number
hook: What do these [X] [objects in image] have in common? / They each are ideas built around [briefly explain concept].

title: A personal branding lesson that's NOT about you
principle: Sharing someone else's remarkable story — with no direct involvement — still transfers some of their credibility to you by association, per the Halo Effect.
best_for: creators building authority in a space who want a "borrowed authority" format — retelling an inspiring outsider's story to align themselves with impressive values before they have their own case study to lean on.
requires: a real named individual's biography with a direct quote and specific career turning points
hook: She/He [made unconventional decision] at [age]. By [later age], [impressive outcome]. / Meet [Full Name], [role/title].

title: Not your typical LinkedIn "Glow-Up" story
principle: Your story's timeline doesn't have to move for it to land — stick to one moment in time and contrast two conflicting elements, letting the reader arrive at the conclusion themselves before you reveal what you learned (show-then-tell).
best_for: prospects with an unusual dual background (two roles or experiences held at once) who want a distinctive origin story that doesn't rely on a simple before/after arc.
requires: a specific real memory of holding two contrasting roles/experiences at the same time
hook: [X] years ago, I had 2 very different [roles/experiences]: one [impressive metric], the other [humble metric]. / [Role #1] - [brief description of what it involved].

title: Your client conversations are rich with content ideas
principle: Share what you know regardless of how obvious it may seem to you — it may be a revelation to someone without your level of expertise. Sales calls, client comms, and DMs are a ready-made FAQ bank.
best_for: service providers and consultants who field the same prospect/client questions on repeat and want to convert that expertise into authority-building posts.
requires: the exact real question a client or prospect asked them
note: echoes T14.1's "recently someone asked me" mechanic, more terse/direct in structure.
hook: A [senior person you advise/work with] who's struggling with [specific challenge] just asked me: "[The exact question they asked]" / I've been [doing this thing] since my days [at credible company/role]. And I've [impressive result/metric that demonstrates your expertise].

title: How to inject believability into your stories
principle: Use negative terms, perspectives, and frames to create attention-getting hooks (negativity bias), and pair stories with visual proof — screenshots, photos, documents — so they read as credible, not fabricated.
best_for: creators worried their stories sound too polished or AI-generated; especially useful for consultants who have real DMs, feedback, or documents to back a claim.
requires: the specific blunt feedback a real friend/colleague/mentor gave them, verbatim
hook: One of my [closest friends/colleagues/mentors] told me my [work/output] sucked. / "[Direct quote - the blunt feedback they gave you]."

title: Not sure what to write about? Try this…
principle: "Document, don't create" (Gary Vee) — write to your past self or document a challenge you just overcame; the lessons and steps surface naturally once you sit down and record what actually happened.
best_for: prospects who feel they have "nothing to post about" — early-career professionals or founders who can mine their own recent struggle for material.
requires: a specific past struggle story including one concrete detail like a tracking ritual/tool used
note: echoes T17.1's "build in public / document don't create" principle, applied here to a past struggle rather than a live building process.
hook: When I was getting started as a [role/creator/professional], I was [doing early version of what you do now and explain key thing you did differently]. / I needed [specific number] of [clients/customers/sales] [key reason why].

title: Peer conversations as content
principle: Invite your audience to be a fly on the wall for your real-life conversations — set the scene, introduce characters, share dialogue. AI can't compete with that, and collaboration extends reach when the other person engages back.
best_for: prospects who network heavily with peers or experts and want a low-lift, relationship-building content format that also builds community credibility.
requires: a specific real conversation with a named person including their actual quoted answers
hook: Some of the best [topic] conversations happen over... / [unexpected casual setting].

title: How to write a viral origin story
principle: Compress years of wins and losses into an "Age Timeline" — specific names, results, and ages, each beat starting with a verb — ending on an overarching lesson; grounding impressive feats in humble beginnings makes them relatable.
best_for: prospects with a long, varied career history (founders, executives) who want a fast, high-density origin story instead of one narrow anecdote.
requires: a full personal career timeline with specific ages, wins, losses, and results
hook: Age [X]: [Origin story / starting point]. / Age [X]: [Early attempt]. [Result].

title: Surface-level vs basement-level problems (The Generic Content Trap)
principle: Generic content only touches surface-level problems; dig 3-4 levels deeper into the fears and faulty beliefs underneath, then reframe those unspoken challenges before presenting your solution.
best_for: prospects selling a course, offer, or lead magnet whose audience already "knows" the surface problem — coaches and consultants who need to differentiate through depth of insight, not repeated generic advice.
requires: a specific personal turning point when their skill/results accelerated fastest
note: echoes T18.5 / T7.1's comment-gated lead magnet mechanic in its back half.
hook: I can't stop thinking about a [piece of content] I saw the other day. / It said:

title: How to test an unusual offer (without pitching)
principle: Give an unusual offer a clever, attention-getting name, break down who it's for, what it involves, the problem it tackles, and why it's necessary — then ask the audience directly if they'd want it, turning a post into a low-risk demand test.
best_for: service providers who want to validate a new, non-standard offer (a niche retainer, an unconventional deliverable) before formally building or pitching it.
requires: a specific client's actual price paid and the exact unconventional role they were hired for
hook: A [role/friend/client] paid me [specific price] to be their [unexpected, informal role]. / Not their [expected professional role 1].

title: Why most case study posts fail to convert
principle: If you want people to buy now, show them what they stand to lose by doing nothing — pair a case study with a hard deadline, expiring bonuses, and demand signals to create real urgency.
best_for: prospects launching a cohort, program, or paid offer who have a client result to showcase and need to convert warm readers into buyers, not just admirers.
requires: a named client's specific result, their testimonial quote, and the program's bonus stack details
note: echoes T18.1's named case study mechanic in its opening, but pivots into a bonus-stacked, deadline-driven launch pitch instead of a minimalist verdict.
hook: Merely [timeframe] after joining [your program/offer]... / [Client name] [achieved a specific, impressive result].

title: Let's be blunt about LinkedIn for a sec
principle: Content only earns its keep if it serves a defined goal — get clear on the purpose of each post, then always include a CTA (in the post or top comment) that points to the next logical step in your funnel.
best_for: prospects who post consistently but see no business results and need a documented-framework post that doubles as proof-of-expertise and a funnel driver.
requires: a specific real result they recently achieved and the framework's actual stages
hook: Last week I had a big realisation after [achieving impressive result] (without [conventional constraint/method]): / 1. [First stage of framework]

title: What your prospective customers actually want
principle: People don't buy products — they buy remedies for painful problems, desirable outcomes, and a new identity. Address all three before you ever mention the product.
best_for: prospects selling a course or service where the real value is transformation or identity change, not a feature list — coaches and personal-brand builders in particular.
requires: only general knowledge of audience identity types/behavior patterns, no personal facts
hook: Many [people/group] want [desirable change/outcome]. / But most of them never [identify invisible barrier that holds them back].

title: The boring (but effective) truth about posting on LinkedIn
principle: "Repetition builds recognition" — you don't control who sees any given post, so the most profitable creators repeat the same 10-15 validated ideas rather than chasing constant originality.
best_for: prospects worried about "running out of things to say" — reassures them that repeating validated messages, not novelty, drives recognition and business results.
requires: a specific piece of advice they personally dismissed early on and the mistakes that resulted
hook: I [dismissive reaction] at so much [your field/niche] advice. / (And now I wish I'd listened)

title: Justin Welsh's favourite 6-step persuasive post writing framework (PASTOR)
principle: "Copy is not written. Copy is assembled." (Eugene Schwartz) — great copywriters build posts on proven persuasive skeletons: Problem, Amplify, Story, Transformation, Offer, Response.
best_for: prospects selling an offer or service who need a structured, persuasive post rather than a pure story post — service providers with a clear, nameable buyer pain point.
requires: a specific personal struggle they experienced, with real numbers and feelings
hook: There's nothing worse than [relatable pain point]. / But a lot of [people/group] are in that situation. It sucks.

title: The "timestamp" hook
principle: Contrast two time-stamped moments — a low point and a high point — to plant the unanswered question "How did that happen?" in the reader's mind, then spend the rest of the post answering it.
best_for: prospects with a clear before/after transformation (career pivot, business turnaround) who want an authority-building story hook.
requires: a specific turning-point story including who said what to change their mind
note: echoes T18.2's before/after transformation mechanic and T10.3's transformation-story case study — this version leads with a bare two-line timestamp contrast rather than a metric or milestone list.
hook: [Year]: [Where you struggled or almost gave up] / [Year]: [Where you are now – e.g. same domain, elevated position]

title: "If you're seeing this right now, you're ahead of 99% of people"
principle: Tap into FOMO by teasing a big, time-sensitive opportunity in the hook without revealing what it is until several sentences in — forcing the reader to click "see more" to find out.
best_for: prospects positioning themselves as early or insider voices on a trend (AI, a new platform, a market shift) who want to convert curiosity into authority.
requires: only domain expertise/prediction about a trend, no personal or client facts
hook: We are staring at the BIGGEST opportunity since [recent reference point] and [historical reference point]. If you're seeing this right now, you're ahead of [large percentage] of [people/group]. / This isn't just another [category] post.

title: Announcement Post (rare hype-builder)
principle: Putting something new into the world takes guts, which is why Announcement Posts generate outsized goodwill and support — but they should be used sparingly (roughly once every 90 days) to preserve their impact.
best_for: founders or service providers launching a new offer, product, podcast, or milestone (or announcing a hire or a dream client win) who want a rare, high-impact post rather than routine self-promotion.
requires: project name, origin year, spread examples, and specific launch offer details
hook: I'm finally launching [project type] I should've launched [years/months] ago: / [Project Name].

title: Broad-reach hook (non-niche terms)
principle: Broad, non-niche hook terms (career, hiring, remote work, layoffs, burnout) appeal to the widest possible LinkedIn audience, so they're the right lever when the goal is maximum reach rather than narrow, qualified engagement.
best_for: founders or leaders who are hiring or growing a team and want a company-update post that travels beyond their existing niche audience.
requires: current hiring/building context and the specific traits you're seeking
hook: One of the best things you can do for your [area of life/career/system] is get comfortable [doing this specific thing]: / [Ready-made phrase/unconventional path 1]

title: Common Mistakes format
principle: Highlighting mistakes to avoid taps into loss aversion — people are roughly twice as motivated to avoid a loss as to pursue an equivalent gain — which is why the "common mistakes" format works in virtually any niche.
best_for: consultants or experts who want to demonstrate authority by diagnosing prospects' current mistakes and prescribing the fix, priming readers to self-identify as needing help.
requires: domain expertise, five common niche mistakes and fixes, no personal facts
hook: I see the same [platform/area] [mistakes/problems] every single day: / - [Mistake 1].

title: POV-driven strategy post (content people are starving for in the Age of AI)
principle: Plain tips and frameworks are now a commodity anyone (or any AI) can produce; a raw, lived-experience point of view is what's actually scarce, so leading with your own opinion and story differentiates you from AI-generated content.
best_for: established consultants with a distinctive methodology who want to be seen as a thought leader rather than a generic tips-account, especially those competing against AI-written content.
requires: domain expertise, a general strategy framework for a client type
hook: Your [team/department/strategy] is [driving impressive metric] this year. But your [key person/strategy] is [driving low metric]. / The solution isn't to [obvious but wrong approach] because that just [briefly example why it's a mistake].

title: Curation post
principle: Curating other people's insights or top creators acts as a pressure-release valve that doesn't require sharing your own story every day, builds authority by association, and can boost reach when the mentioned creators engage with the post.
best_for: time-constrained founders or experts who want a reliable, high-reach format for days without a fresh personal insight, while still appearing generous and well-connected.
requires: three named real LinkedIn creators and a summary of what each does
note: echoes T4.1's brief-comparison-image mechanic loosely, but this is the library's only "curate other creators" format — no earlier duplicate.
hook: You don't need an [intimidating credential] to [learn/do desirable thing]. / These [X] LinkedIn creators make it easy for you:

title: Borrowed credibility hook
principle: Naming a specific, high-calibre source (a named client, well-known company, or credible expert) instantly borrows trust the writer hasn't yet earned outright — readers judge credibility by association before they judge the content itself.
best_for: consultants or coaches who've worked with recognisable clients or companies and want to open a post with instant authority instead of a vague "a client of mine" claim.
requires: a named client's exact question plus specific trends found in your results
hook: [Time period ago], [individual/company] told me: / [Briefly explain their question/goal/problem].

title: Terrifying (present-tense) vulnerability
principle: Present-tense, in-the-moment vulnerability ("I feel like a fraud right now") is rarer and more magnetic than past-tense, resolved vulnerability, because it lets readers recognise themselves in an unresolved struggle rather than a tidy success story.
best_for: founders or professionals navigating a genuinely uncertain moment (a leap, a launch, a fear) who want to build deep reader loyalty through raw, real-time honesty rather than polished retrospection.
requires: a specific real present-tense moment, physical location, and vulnerable internal question
hook: [Time period ago] I watched [vivid image of someone else doing something noteworthy]. Meanwhile, I couldn't shake the [thing pulling me back to my own world / [Briefly share a relevant detail that brings this moment to life].

title: Viral giveaway / lead magnet post
principle: Offering a free, high-value resource in exchange for a comment (then DM-ing a landing page) converts LinkedIn attention directly into email subscribers, because a tangible free asset motivates action far more than a generic "follow for more."
best_for: service providers or consultants who already have (or can quickly build) a lead magnet and want a proven, high-converting format to grow their email list alongside LinkedIn reach.
requires: real giveaway assets with proof numbers and an actual social-proof result
note: echoes T18.5 / T7.1 / T5.2's comment-gated lead magnet mechanic — this version anchors the value stack on time invested collecting the resources rather than a client-results portfolio.
hook: I spent [time frame] collecting [X] [resources/tools] to help you: / * [Desirable outcome 1]

title: Flat, unemotional hook for gut-punch stories
principle: Stripping emotional language out of a hook ("My coworker got the promotion over me" instead of "I was devastated") leaves room for the reader to inject their own feelings — the less emotion the writer performs, the more emotion the reader actually feels.
best_for: anyone with an injustice, setback, or comeback story who wants a story post that hits harder than an emotionally over-narrated version — useful for building a memorable personal narrative.
requires: a real injustice/setback story and the exact dismissive quote received
hook: [Someone else] got the [thing you deserved] over me. / [Their weakness]. [Their one advantage].

title: 90-day re-introduction post
principle: Even long-standing followers and connections know very little about you and forget over time, so periodically re-stating who you are, what you sell, and how you got here rebuilds the familiarity that breeds trust.
best_for: established creators or founders with a growing audience who haven't recently restated their offer, story, and goal — a recurring quarterly post that catches up newer followers who missed the origin story.
requires: a personal origin story, prior identity and how the journey started
note: echoes T16.1's "what a post written by an actual human looks like" identity-facts mechanic, but this version is structured around the business (offer, channels, tools) rather than personal quirks.
hook: I'm [age], [nationality], [personality trait/fact], and run a [brief business descriptor]. / Last [time period ago], [specific metric/accolade achieved].

title: Withheld-information story (mystery hook)
principle: Deliberately withholding details (like who "this massive creator" is) keeps the focus on the feeling of a story rather than the facts, and leaves room for the reader's imagination to fill the gaps — mystery makes stories more gripping than full disclosure.
best_for: storytellers with a specific pivotal-decision narrative (turning down an opportunity, a career-defining choice) who want to build suspense rather than over-explain every detail.
requires: a specific real turned-down opportunity and the true reason for hesitating
hook: [Timeframe] ago, I walked away from a career-making opportunity. / And I've never felt more at peace with a decision.

title: Building-in-public value prop reminder
principle: Most followers won't visit your profile to learn what you do, so content needs to double as free advertising — organically reminding people of your value prop through wins, relatable moments, and education rather than a direct pitch.
best_for: founders or agency owners building a new project in public who want to remind their audience what their core business does while telling an authentic in-progress story.
requires: a real project milestone/metric and the specific build-in-public strategy used
note: echoes T17.1's build-in-public mechanic — this earlier version leans harder on the value-prop reminder, T17.1 leans harder on the three-question idea engine.
hook: My brand new [project / channel / initiative] just hit [early milestone]. / But [metric] isn't the interesting part…

title: "You know that feeling when..." sensory device
principle: Describing the reader's problem state with a concrete, physical metaphor ("simple tasks feel like climbing a mountain") rather than an abstract label ("being unproductive") makes the reader feel seen in their bones, not just understood intellectually.
best_for: coaches or consultants writing relatable pain-point posts who want the reader to viscerally recognise their own struggle before a framework or solution is pitched.
requires: a specific real break from work and the pivotal moment ending it
hook: I stepped away from [activity / project / responsibility] for [time period]. / No [related task A], [related task B], or [related task C].

title: The Qualification Sandwich
principle: A bold, unhedged claim risks sounding preachy, but immediately following it with a brief line of self-awareness ("not against them, I post them too") signals honesty without undercutting the original point — readers trust claims that acknowledge their own nuance.
best_for: opinionated experts who want to make strong, contrarian claims about industry practices without alienating the audience who still does the thing being critiqued.
requires: a stated industry opinion and a real benefit from the alternative approach
hook: I'm seeing [platform / craft / industry shift]. / (and [share quick opinion])

title: Be remembered, not just seen
principle: As LinkedIn's reach declines and the barrier to posting drops, competing purely for visibility is a losing game — the real advantage comes from being clearly remembered and understood for the specific problem you solve, not from raw reach.
best_for: experienced creators or consultants past the growth-hacking phase who want to sharpen positioning and message clarity rather than chase impression counts.
requires: domain expertise, a general industry-shift observation and positioning stance
hook: [Target audience/peer group] never [challenge common belief]. / It was just easier to believe we did when [explain old dynamic].

title: The AIDA copywriting formula
principle: AIDA works because it grabs Attention with a belief-shattering hook, holds Interest with concrete steps, stirs Desire with tangible new possibilities, then calls the reader to Action.
best_for: coaches and consultants challenging a piece of conventional wisdom in their niche, who want to move a reader from mindset shift to a concrete next action.
requires: domain expertise, generic platform actions and outcomes, no personal facts
hook: It's impossible to [achieve a common goal] on/in [platform/tool/group] today. / Instead, here's what's achievable today:

title: How to get eyeballs on your long-form content
principle: Borrowing credibility from a well-known guest or source primes the reader to trust the tips that follow, before you've even made your own case.
best_for: creators repurposing a podcast episode or long-form asset who want to drive traffic to it using someone else's authority.
requires: a named guest and their real specific tips from an actual asset
hook: [Person's name] [has done a remarkable thing] with [topic/product]. Here's how they [approach specific skill]: / 1. [Practical tip shared in long-form content]

title: The Slippery Slide Effect
principle: Ultra-short, incomplete opening sentences pull readers down the page before they can bounce — each line's only job is to get you to read the next one.
best_for: thought leaders building anticipation for an upcoming book, course, or framework who want a hook built on rhythm rather than information density.
requires: domain expertise, general conceptual musing and a future-content tease
hook: [Concept 1] = [Outcome 1]. [Concept 2] = [Outcome 2]. / It's not the [concept 1/desire] we want. It's the [deeper desire].

title: "LinkedIn loves stories"
principle: Short transformation stories work when they combine transformation, relatability (humble beginnings), and inspiration (overcoming common obstacles) in just a handful of sentences.
best_for: founders or experts with a genuine rags-to-results origin story who want an evergreen credibility-through-journey post.
requires: a specific real origin story, hometown, hardship, and how you escaped it
note: echoes T18.2 / T10.3 / T4.4's before/after transformation mechanic — this is the library's most stripped-down, sentence-level version.
hook: I grew up here. / [Share 1-2 details of living circumstances and/or location]

title: Warning: this post may get you worked up!
principle: Every good story needs a villain — naming a clear source of conflict early raises the emotional stakes and gets readers invested.
best_for: service providers who've experienced workplace or industry dysfunction (bad managers, broken systems) and want to channel that frustration into a relatable, high-engagement post.
requires: a specific real workplace dysfunction situation with concrete issues experienced
note: echoes T13.1's "your content needs an enemy" principle, in its earliest/rawest form in the library.
hook: Once upon a time. / I [experienced a challenging and slightly unusual situation]:

title: The PAS copywriting formula
principle: Problem-Agitate-Solve works because it empathizes with the reader's pain, intensifies the tension, then relieves it with a concrete remedy — a satisfying resolution arc.
best_for: consultants or coaches selling a solution to a well-known pain point (e.g. overthinking, procrastination) who want a proven persuasion structure.
requires: domain expertise, generic facts, consequence, and tips for a pain point
hook: [Give an impressive, relatable fact]. / [Give another fact that builds on the first].

title: Don't do this… instead, do this…
principle: Naming a striking personal result upfront pre-empts the "why should I listen to you" objection and earns credibility before the advice lands.
best_for: consultants positioning themselves against common but ineffective approaches in their space, who want to contrast bad tactics with their better method.
requires: a specific real recent unusual event plus concrete alternative strategies
hook: This week, I [experienced a remarkable/unusual event]. / Here are [X] ways I wouldn't recommend to [related activity]:

title: How to build anticipation for a new product
principle: Sharing the failure-before-success origin of a product builds trust and anticipation, because readers become emotionally invested once they see the standards behind it.
best_for: founders or creators launching a product, course, or service who want to build a pre-launch waitlist through narrative rather than a hard pitch.
requires: a real struggle/challenge story from building the product before launch
hook: I'm [feeling/emotion]. It's a big [day/week/month]. / On [day/date], I'm launching [product/service].

title: How to lead with vulnerability and inspire others
principle: Vivid, sensory word choices dramatize a struggle-recovery story far more effectively than plain factual language, making the vulnerability land emotionally.
best_for: founders or service providers with a genuine setback (bankruptcy, business failure) they're ready to share as proof that comebacks are possible.
requires: a specific real business failure/comeback story with concrete repercussions
hook: [X years] ago, my [type of venture] failed. / Despite not having [type of support], I was determined to succeed.

title: Good strategy → great strategy
principle: Laying out a clear amateur-to-expert progression (in quoted "levels") shows readers exactly what separates surface-level effort from mastery, positioning the writer at the top tier.
best_for: consultants or coaches who want to reframe a common but shallow tactic as insufficient and position their fuller methodology as the expert-level answer.
requires: domain expertise, generic amateur-to-expert framework, no personal facts
hook: Amateur: "I [basic activity] [on/with] [Platform/Product/Strategy]." / Intermediate:

title: How to celebrate a win (without bragging)
principle: You can share a win without bragging by starting with your humble starting point, crediting others before mentioning the achievement, then redirecting the spotlight back to the reader.
best_for: consultants or founders announcing a milestone (revenue, recognition, a feature) who want social proof without sounding self-congratulatory.
requires: a specific start date, real early struggles, and a named org/person who recognized the work
hook: I [started engaging with specific action] on [date].  / At first, I [briefly list common experiences/initial failures/struggles].

title: "Pssst… wanna know a secret?"
principle: Promising a "secret" triggers curiosity because withheld information feels exclusive — but the payoff must be genuinely useful or the reader feels cheated.
best_for: coaches or consultants whose real "secret" is disciplined repetition of a simple daily habit, and who want a curiosity-hook post that still delivers concrete steps.
requires: a specific daily habit and the achieved outcome it actually produced
hook: People ask me how I [achieved desirable outcome] so quickly. / My secret?

title: What promise are you making to the reader?
principle: Opening a story with the promise of a "lesson" the reader will gain gives them a concrete reason to keep reading, since every post is implicitly competing for attention.
best_for: creators telling a networking or serendipity story who want to frame it around a payoff for the reader, not just personal reminiscence.
requires: a specific person met at a real event and the real chain of events that followed
hook: I [achieved remarkable outcome] [through unexpected means]. / [X years/months] ago, I [met/supported someone] at [event/scenario].

title: Pair your advice with credibility elements
principle: Naming your advice as a formal "rule" or principle (rather than presenting it as raw opinion) lends legitimacy and makes it feel earned rather than improvised.
best_for: coaches with a large following who still need to earn trust with each new reader — useful for turning a repeatable piece of advice into a named, shareable framework.
requires: only a named principle/rule and generic supporting advice, no personal specifics needed
note: echoes T11.1's "boring truth" named-framework mechanic and T7.4's named-concept mechanic.
hook: [Name of Rule/Wisdom]: / [Context] is tough. [Setbacks] happen.

title: Are you making this mistake?
principle: Mistake-hooks work because they trigger loss aversion — readers stop to check whether they're one of the majority making the error, which is what earns the read-through.
best_for: consultants who see a widespread, correctable mistake in their audience's current behaviour and want a high-attention hook to introduce the fix.
requires: a specific statistic on how many people make the named mistake
note: echoes T3.3's "Common Mistakes" mechanic — this is a compressed, single-mistake version rather than a 5-mistake listicle.
hook: [High number]% of [digital asset/group] make this mistake: / Did you know by [following common practice], you are actually [eliciting negative outcome]?

title: How to create "valuable" content
principle: Value content works like a bridge from a reader's current problem to a desirable outcome — giving a clear, structured roadmap (not just information) is what actually makes content feel "valuable."
best_for: coaches and consultants selling a repeatable method or system who need to prove they have a concrete process, not just motivation, for prospects to follow.
requires: a specific quantifiable goal, a named strategy, and the real results it produced
hook: [Specific quantifiable goal]/[short timeframe] = [Specific quantifiable goal] in [long timeframe] / That's the goal.

title: Why you should give more examples
principle: Abstract ideas only become useful once paired with a concrete example — examples make concepts visual, relatable and memorable, engaging the reader's intuitive brain alongside the logical one.
best_for: subject-matter experts explaining research-backed or conceptual ideas (psychology, strategy, behavioral science) who need to make dry findings feel tangible and applicable.
requires: a specific research finding or study backing the named psychological concept
note: echoes T15.4's "why you should give more examples" template name and principle directly — this earlier version is built around a single named phenomenon rather than a portfolio review/audit.
hook: [Startling fact or statistic] / But why [relevant question/problem]?

title: How to fix BROKEN thinking
principle: People become receptive to your solution faster when you first name the misconception they already hold, showing you "get them" before you reframe the problem.
best_for: consultants and freelancers correcting a common client misunderstanding about their industry or service (e.g. pricing, retainers, engagement models).
requires: only domain expertise on the common misconception and a general reframe strategy
hook: Why does [specific audience] face [common problem]? / Because they believe [common misconception].

title: Here's a reality check for ya!
principle: Negativity bias makes blunt, myth-busting language ("can't fix") grab more attention than positive framing — naming your limits builds trust because it feels honest rather than salesy.
best_for: service providers and specialists who need to manage unrealistic client expectations upfront and filter out bad-fit prospects.
requires: only domain expertise on realistic limits of the role/industry, no client specifics
hook: "[Industry/Role], [unrealistic request]." / X things [Industry/Role] can't fix:

title: How to champion a hero in a brand's success story
principle: A rise-fall-pivot-rise arc with a named "hero" turns a case study into a story people want to finish, letting the strategic lesson land emotionally instead of just informationally.
best_for: agencies and consultants wanting to turn a client turnaround or case study into a compelling, ghostwritable brand narrative.
requires: a named brand's real strategy, specific industry shift, and turnaround metrics
note: echoes T13.4's "named concept" client-transformation case study — this version tells a brand's own turnaround rather than a coach's client story.
hook: [Brand's success story] is a testament to [key strategy]. [Impressive metric]. / Let's dive into the journey:

title: Empower your reader to think differently
principle: Opening with a surprising statistic earns the right to challenge a widely-held belief about success, then handing the reader permission to define success on their own terms.
best_for: coaches and consultants working with high-achievers who feel boxed in by conventional definitions of success (exits, titles, status).
requires: a specific statistic on how few people/initiatives hit the typical success bar
hook: Only [a small fraction] of [specific initiatives/individuals] [achieve desirable outcome]. / You don't have to follow [typical definition of success].

title: "You've been lied to. Here's the truth…"
principle: Bold, polarising "harsh truth" statements outperform balanced takes because they force a reaction; reversing a common false assumption is a repeatable engine for new content ideas.
best_for: specialists positioning against a widely-held but wrong belief in their field — good for attracting an audience that feels "finally, someone gets it."
requires: only a contrarian industry opinion and general reasoning, no personal specifics needed
hook: [Specific harsh truth]. / [Necessary action/belief] is essential to [achieve desirable outcome].

title: "Hot off the press! Here's what you need to know…"
principle: Being first to distill a long, boring announcement into a short, opinionated breakdown earns attention and authority as the go-to interpreter of industry news.
best_for: founders or experts positioned as industry commentators who want to ride news-jacking moments (launches, funding, platform updates).
requires: a real, specific news event or product launch from a named company
hook: BREAKING: [Short time period ago], [High-profile person/company/collaboration] revealed [new product/service/news] / Here's what you need to know:

title: How to boost your authority by association
principle: Publicly crediting a collaborator's journey alongside your own borrows and lends credibility in both directions — authority by association.
best_for: consultants and agency owners who want to showcase partnerships or peer relationships to build trust with prospects who value network signals.
requires: a specific named collaborator, how they met, and a real shared anecdote/turning point
hook: [Short time period ago], I [met/achieved significant milestone with] [description of the person – e.g. a rising star in the tech industry] / We first connected in [initial meeting context] in [year].

title: To sell more, acknowledge and resolve objections
principle: Naming a prospect's specific fear before they voice it disarms resistance and builds trust faster than ignoring the objection.
best_for: service providers or founders selling a product/service with a common, predictable objection (price, effort, credibility, tech-adoption fear).
requires: a specific product name plus two named people/companies actually using it
hook: "I don't want [common fear or misconception]." / [Reassure reader]

title: Can you tell WHY this post went viral?
principle: Stacking credibility (a title like "3x Founder"), an industry-agnostic hook with provocative negativity-biased language, a relatable frustration, and a short actionable fix is the anatomy of a viral post.
best_for: founders or operators with a credible title who want to call out an industry blind spot and offer a memorable, contrarian fix.
requires: only a general strategy-comparison framework, no personal or client specifics needed
hook: The difference between [strategy A] and [strategy B] is:  / [Key negative outcome associated with strategy B that's often overlooked].

title: How to use analogies to make your point
principle: An absurd but accurate analogy exposes an unfair or illogical industry norm faster than a direct argument, because the comparison does the persuading for you.
best_for: freelancers and service providers who need to push back on a common unfair client ask (free work, scope creep, undervaluing expertise).
requires: only an analogy and domain reasoning about an unfair industry norm
hook: "[Common but controversial business practice posed as a statement by uninformed culprit]" / Wait a minute.

title: Boost your credibility and relatability with shared experiences
principle: Naming the reader's starting point and admitting "I've been there too" builds instant trust before you introduce the harder truth and your solution.
best_for: coaches and consultants targeting a specific audience segment (e.g. early-stage freelancers) where "I was you" is a credible, relatable opener.
requires: a specific real-life example of someone applying the proposed solution
hook: Many [target audience] start [at common starting point].  / And that makes sense.

title: The problem with attention-grabbing phrases
principle: Calling out overused, trend-chasing content tactics — and explaining the psychology behind why they work — positions you as more thoughtful than competitors chasing the same clichés.
best_for: experienced creators or consultants differentiating themselves from a saturated field of copycat content.
requires: only domain commentary on overused content tactics and a named alternative approach
hook: [Pose a common concern as a question]? / - [Problematic trend 1]

title: The power of repeating yourself over and over and over again
principle: Repeating an identical sentence structure builds rhythm and tension, making the eventual "here's all you actually need" payoff land harder by contrast with everything it excludes.
best_for: anyone selling a simplified, no-fluff method against a market full of complicated alternatives.
requires: a specific real achievement and the prerequisites actually skipped to reach it
note: echoes T9.4's parallel-repetition structure and T8.1's list-stacking mechanic, applied here to a founder's no-prerequisites brag list.
hook: I [achieved goal Y] without [common pre-requisite 1].   / I [achieved goal Y] without [common pre-requisite 2].

title: Remember to document your journey
principle: Contrasting where you are now against where you started turns your own growth into proof and content, building trust through demonstrated progress rather than claimed expertise.
