hook: [Ask a thought-provoking question or present a common challenge].   / [Briefly explain or imply why you're qualified to answer this question].

title: A Great Way To Dramatise Your Writing
principle: Anaphora (repeating a phrase at the start of successive lines) injects rhythm and momentum into writing, making a contrarian argument feel more forceful and memorable.
best_for: consultants making a bold, contrarian argument against a conventional mindset who want their writing to feel punchier and more quotable.
requires: only a contrarian opinion and generic illustrative examples, no personal facts
note: echoes T-LC13.2's anaphora mechanic directly — this version applies the device to a contrarian argument rather than a positive-action pivot.
hook: [Bold, contrarian statement that challenges conventional thinking].   / [Use short, rhythmic sentences to highlight the problems with this mindset or system].

title: Is Your Advice Actually Actionable, Though?
principle: Sharing an idea from a book or framework isn't enough — translating each principle into a concrete, applied step for your specific context is what makes advice actionable instead of abstract.
best_for: consultants who reference frameworks, books, or research in their content and need to turn "interesting ideas" into practical, applied takeaways for their niche.
requires: only domain knowledge of a framework/book translated into practical audience-specific steps
hook: I've [explored] many [ideas/resources/approaches], but this one [unlocked benefit]: / (And it's not [commonly spoken about idea/resource/approach])

title: Digital Word Of Mouth (WOM)
principle: Client testimonials are more persuasive than self-made claims because they act as social proof — showcasing a happy customer's words shows prospects the offer works for people like them.
best_for: service providers and consultants who have real client wins or testimonials and need a natural, non-salesy way to share a success story without sounding like an ad.
requires: a specific client testimonial, success story, or milestone to share
note: the shortest and most understated of the library's testimonial-led templates (compare T10.4's "bare testimonial screenshot" and T-LC22.5's full case study).
hook: I don't do this often. / But I had to share it…

title: How To Work Smarter, Not Harder
principle: Telling an audience to stop an ineffective, widely-practiced habit and replace it with a smarter alternative works because it names a shared frustration before offering relief.
best_for: consultants challenging an outdated industry habit (e.g. constantly creating new content instead of repurposing, or manual processes instead of systems) who want to position a smarter alternative.
requires: only a contrarian opinion about an outdated common practice and its smarter alternative
note: echoes T-LC28.3's "don't play the game" and T-LC19.1's "don't X, start Y" family.
hook: Please STOP [doing common and/or ineffective practice]. / I see too many [examples of people/businesses doing this] that [describe the negative outcome], yet they're still [repeating the ineffective practice].

title: All Top 1% Creators Understand This
principle: Contrast (old vs. new, struggle vs. triumph, ethical vs. unethical) is a literary device that makes stories more vivid, persuasive, and memorable because our brains are wired to notice differences.
best_for: consultants with a strong story about someone significant (a mentor, parent, or client) whose values or approach contrasted sharply with another party, teaching a lesson through that tension.
requires: a specific story about a mentor/parent/client, including an actual quote they said
hook: A story [from someone significant or memorable]. / If you're [a relevant audience], this might resonate with you as it did with me.

title: Reframing Negative Perspectives
principle: Naming a reader's mental roadblocks makes them feel understood and builds trust, and reframing those same fears into positive perspectives leaves them optimistic and more open to acting.
best_for: coaches and consultants whose prospects are held back by an outdated mindset (e.g. about career, money, or process) that needs reframing more than new information.
requires: a specific personal or client example with a starting metric and improved result
note: echoes T-LC15.2's dispel-false-beliefs mechanic and T16.5's future-pacing negative framing, applied here to a timeline contrast.
hook: [Year/Timeframe 1]: [Something common or traditional people did] / [Year/Timeframe 2]: [How the practice has shifted or evolved]

title: Wanna Make (More) Money On LinkedIn? Read This
principle: Naming the specific person, characteristic, and struggle you help with (rather than chasing broad engagement) builds trust because readers see themselves reflected in the challenges you describe, making the eventual insight feel earned and relevant.
best_for: ghostwriting prospects who are burning time on LinkedIn without converting attention into revenue and need to reposition their content around a defined ICP rather than vanity metrics.
requires: only domain knowledge of the ICP's common characteristics and challenges
hook: Over the past [timeframe], I've talked to [group of people] that [share common characteristic or achievement] but struggle with [specific issue]. / They genuinely want to [unlock desirable outcome].

title: How To Twist The Knife (Making A Problem Hurt)
principle: Naming a problem and then vividly listing its painful, specific symptoms makes the reader FEEL the pain viscerally, turning the eventual solution from a nice-to-have into a life raft.
best_for: consultants and coaches whose prospects already sense a problem but haven't felt its full weight — useful for deepening emotional buy-in before pitching a reframe or offer.
requires: only domain expertise naming a problem's symptoms and a reframe with advice
note: echoes T-LC16.2's "twist the knife" FOMO mechanic directly, expanded into a fuller advice-and-reframe structure.
hook: If you're [target audience/aspiring group], you've probably felt this: / [Common pain point].

title: How To Stand Out (Without Ruining Your Rep)
principle: Naming and rejecting generic, watered-down conventional wisdom before offering bolder, more specific advice signals confidence and expertise, prompting engagement from people who agree and disagree alike.
best_for: founders and experts positioned as thought leaders in a crowded niche who want to differentiate with a contrarian, opinionated stance rather than blend in with safe advice.
requires: only a contrarian opinion rejecting common advice with bolder alternative actions
hook: Most [field or industry] advice is [adjective 1]. / And [adjective 2].

title: Every Creator Should Use These (Advanced)
principle: Framing a milestone with a self-deprecating counterpoint before delivering a concrete, numbered lesson makes advice feel hard-won and credible rather than boastful, which builds the trust lead magnets depend on.
best_for: consultants and service providers who want to promote a lead magnet or resource but need a humble, story-driven on-ramp so the pitch doesn't feel salesy.
requires: a specific achieved milestone plus a real humbling anecdote or lesson behind it
hook: I've [achieved specific success or milestone] in the last [short timeframe]. / But [counterpoint that diminishes the milestone's value].

title: A Hook Tactic For 2025 (And Beyond)
principle: Tying advice to a specific year makes content feel timely and current, tapping into readers' psychological pull toward fresh starts and resolutions — a hook device that works especially well (but not exclusively) around the new year.
best_for: any ghostwriting client wanting a reliable, repeatable hook format for listicle-style posts that need to feel urgent and current rather than evergreen and generic.
requires: only a general listicle of habits to stop, no personal specifics needed
hook: X [negative habits/practices] to eliminate in [timeframe]. / ([Motivational statement about the benefit of change]).

title: A Surefire Way To Improve Your Writing
principle: Adding specificity — vivid language, sensory detail, strong verbs, and hard numbers — makes writing believable and energetic instead of vague, because concrete detail is what proves credibility and expertise.
best_for: subject-matter experts and consultants who want a repeatable framework post that showcases a specific mistake they see often and positions their methodology as the fix.
requires: only a common mistake observed and a named framework with generic example
hook: [Opening line that establishes credibility or introduces an insight]. / [Concise, impactful statement reinforcing the main idea].

title: A Trick To Fire Up Your Reader's Brain
principle: Peppering posts with reflective questions turns passive readers into active participants, helping them self-diagnose their own problems rather than just receiving advice — which deepens engagement and retention.
best_for: coaches and consultants whose value proposition is helping clients make better decisions, since reflective questions mirror the diagnostic conversations they'd have in a session.
requires: only general coaching knowledge to write reflective diagnostic questions
hook: [Common frustration or challenge]. / And as a [target audience], [briefly state why this issue is especially relevant].

title: Unsure What To Write? Try This
principle: Writing to your past self — recounting a piece of blunt feedback or a recent struggle and how you solved it — turns lived experience into distilled, practical content, which builds authority through demonstrated problem-solving rather than abstract advice.
best_for: ghostwriting prospects with writer's block or a thin idea pipeline, especially those who receive frequent client/sales feedback that can be reverse-engineered into lessons.
requires: a specific real anecdote plus the exact quote of feedback that triggered it
note: echoes T6.3's "inject believability with negative feedback" mechanic — this version pivots to a numbered strategy list rather than a repair-plan close.
hook: Had a bit of a wake up call. / [Brief anecdote or situation that led to the realisation].

title: A Timeless Copywriting Technique
principle: The "Slippery Slide Effect" — short punchy opening sentences, tight paragraphs, and simple words — lightens cognitive load so readers glide down the page from the first line, increasing the odds they reach the substance of the post.
best_for: any ghostwriting client who has a real transformation story or framework to share but whose current writing is dense or hard to read; especially useful as a style template for opening hooks.
requires: a specific framework they discovered and the concrete transformation/result it produced
note: echoes T-LC1.3's "Slippery Slide Effect" directly — same named device, this version wraps it around a framework-discovery arc instead of an anticipation-building tease.
hook: Most [people/group] [make common mistake]. / They think they need:

title: 7 Reasons Why This Post Went Viral
principle: Combining a breaking-news hook, insider perspective, clear expectations upfront (what/take/why/what-to-do), specific examples, and a deeper resource offer stacks multiple attention and credibility devices into one post, maximizing both reach and lead capture.
best_for: founders or executives positioned as industry insiders who can credibly comment on a breaking development (a product launch, industry shift, or event) and want to convert that timely commentary into a resource opt-in.
requires: specific facts about a real breaking event/product and their direct hands-on experience with it
note: echoes T-LC5.3 / T-LC28.1's "breaking news" mechanic — this is the most structured version, with an explicit WHAT/MY THOUGHTS/WHY IT MATTERS/WHAT TO DO framework.
hook: BREAKING: [Industry update/product launch/significant event]. / [Briefly state what qualifies you to speak on the subject – e.g. refer to the time spent testing a new product; perhaps you attended an event, or met and obtained insights from noteworthy people].
